## What you'll learn

::: {.concept-card}
[In plain language]{.card-title}
A clear mental model of how ML works without math overload — and where it helps (and where it doesn't) in architectural workflows.
:::

- the 12 principles that make ML predictable, not mysterious
- how to use generative tools responsibly for studio work
- everything reproducible: prompts, seeds, masks, versions

::: {.grading-note}
This is the skinned summary. The full detailed deck — pipeline, diffusion, segmentation, surrogate modeling, GH/Honeybee tooling — is the [original ML for Architecture PDF](../data/ML_for_Architecture_Combined.pdf).
:::

## How to read each principle

Every principle uses the same four-part frame — the same shape as the course's own evidence logic:

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} the principle itself
:::
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} what it changes for you
:::
::::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} how it shows up in design
:::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} apply it to your project
:::
::::

---

## Principle 1 — ML learns a mapping from examples, not rules

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} An ML model is a function f(x) → y whose parameters are fit from examples (x, y).
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Expect pattern recognition, not hand-coded logic. The model learns regularities present in the data.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} (massing image) → predicted daylight metric; (facade photo) → style label.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Name three inputs you could give a model in your current studio project. What output would you want?
:::

---

## Principle 2 — Data is the design brief

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} The dataset defines what the model can and cannot learn.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Better data beats fancier models — curate for coverage and quality, not just quantity.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} A facade-style classifier fails if trained only on one region or era.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} List two gaps in a "facade" dataset that would cause failures on your campus. How would you fill them?
:::

---

## Principle 3 — Representation shapes what can be learned

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} How we encode inputs (pixels, meshes, graphs, text) determines what the model can "see".
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Choosing a representation is like selecting a drawing type: plan vs section vs perspective.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} Street photos (pixels) for segmentation vs adjacency graphs for layout optimization.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} For your task, would pixels, vectors, meshes, or text be best — and why?
:::

---

## Principle 4 — Loss = what "better" means

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} The loss function translates "good" into math; models only improve on what loss rewards.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} If the loss ignores safety or legibility, the model will too. This is your threshold, made explicit.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} A daylight surrogate with MSE learns averages; worst-case glare needs a different objective.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Write a one-line "loss" for your project (e.g., minimize peak glare while keeping daylight autonomy above target).
:::

---

## Principle 5 — Training = reduce loss (gradient descent)

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Training iteratively adjusts parameters in the direction that reduces loss.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Explains learning rate, convergence, and why training looks rough before it stabilizes.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} Don't judge early iterations; monitor the validation curve, not the first guesses.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Sketch how you'd know training is "done" (hint: validation loss / early stopping).
:::

---

## Principle 6 — Generalization is the goal

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} We care about performance on new, unseen data — not just the training set.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Overfitting = memorization; good models transfer to the next site or city.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} A roof-type detector perfect on your curated set fails on cloudy days.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Name two differences between training images and deployment images. How will you test generalization?
:::

---

## Principle 7 — Bias–variance: too simple vs too specific

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Underfit models are too simple; overfit models memorize noise.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} You control this via model capacity, augmentation, and regularization.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} A tiny model misses brick vs terracotta; a huge model memorizes specific buildings.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Which knob would you turn first to reduce overfit — augmentation, regularization, or more data?
:::

---

## Principle 8 — Uncertainty is real: treat outputs as suggestions

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Predictions are probabilistic; confidence varies by context and input quality.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} This is the course thesis in ML form: sample multiple outputs and critique; avoid single-image "truth".
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} Use seeds and A/B comparisons for renders, not one lucky frame.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Generate 3 variations (same seed + small prompt tweaks); choose and justify one.
:::

---

## Principle 9 — Distribution shift breaks models

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} When deployment data differ from training (climate, culture, camera), expect failure.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Plan pilots on real sites; monitor drift; retrain when needed.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} A Berlin-trained segmenter struggles in Bangkok (materials, colors, sky).
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Write one "shift" you expect in your project and a way to detect it.
:::

---

## Principle 10 — Generative models = distributions + conditioning

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Diffusion models learn a distribution and sample from it; prompts/masks/refs condition the sampling.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Prompts steer; seeds give reproducibility; masks and references preserve geometry and identity.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} Keep geometry via masks; change cladding via prompt; reuse the same seed for versions.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Take a white-model view; list what you'd mask vs what you'd let the model change.
:::

---

## Principle 11 — Evaluation must match the task

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Pick metrics that reflect the goal and pair them with human A/B judgment for visuals.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} Numbers alone can reward "pretty wrong" results.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} For concept imagery, use pairwise preference + a rubric (material legibility, camera plausibility).
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Draft two rubric criteria to compare two generated facade images.
:::

---

## Principle 12 — Ethics, IP, and human-in-the-loop

::: {.concept-card}
[Idea]{.card-title} Datasets carry bias; licenses and privacy matter; designers remain accountable.
:::
:::: {.two-col}
::: {.reflection-card}
[Why it matters]{.card-title} You choose sources, cite them, disclose process, and keep clients safe.
:::
::: {.example-card}
[Studio example]{.card-title} Use open/owned references; document prompts, seeds, masks; avoid identifying people without consent.
:::
::::
::: {.activity-card}
[Quick activity · 2 min]{.card-title} Pick one slide of your own and add a visible credit line for every image source.
:::

## Beyond the principles (in the full deck)

The [original PDF](../data/ML_for_Architecture_Combined.pdf) carries the applied half:

- the supervised-learning pipeline, gradient descent, and diffusion, with diagrams
- parametric vs ML vs optimization, and how to combine them
- generative AI operations and a Midjourney vs Nano Banana comparison
- hybrid workflows: massing → render, site analysis via segmentation
- **surrogate modeling** and real tooling: Honeybee/Ladybug, the Owl GH ML plugin

::: {.reflection-card}
Use it as the reference when a studio decision actually needs an ML or generative step — then bring the result to a Session 2 walk-through and audit it.
:::
